As someone who has experienced two completely different kinds of panic attack take anything you find in the thread with a grain of salt.

Would you say it was a more physiological panic attack with heavy breathing, dissiness, and passing out; or was it more like an emotional break down?

The first one is an issue of calmness. Calm them down, get them to breath slow, make sure they aren't opperating any heavy machinary, stop talking to them because talking encourages hyperventalation. Here's my experience with these. I first got one durring a very freaky procedure at the doctors. I woke up not realizing what had happened, nearly punched out a doctor cause I had no clue where I was when I woke up. First time anything like that ever happend to me. I was warned that having one of these increases the odds of it happening again and that was right. For about the next few months I had a few near ones. The key I want to say about these is because they arn't emotional in anyway it can be hard to see it comming even for the person getting one. One second you're driving, then next you realize you could pass out. Talking to a passenger while driving is probably the perfect storm because you have so much destracting you you can't see it coming. Luckily this was very much short term for me. It is very much more physiological than psychological. Basically the body lowers the amount of stress/stimulation it can recieve before it decides to shutdown. For me that was temporary. For others I guess that can be a permenent problem.

The other kind I can't give you any tips for cause I don't know if what produced the onset was clinical or environmental. Even if I did know it's not like I have a magic bullet for you. Showing him emotional support is the only advice I can give you there, and yes that likely will help.

So to sum: The second is a source of psychologically endused stress. Figure out how to help them cope. The first is a reduction in capacity to handle stimuli. Reduce their stimuli.
